note: Swappable grammar pack (R46, §9.3/§9.11) for the serverless functions line. Machine-checked wall between namespaces: 'decision' strings appear while the player decides or loses (labels, terms, refusals, alerts, status rungs) and stay SOBER per §9.3 clauses 2-3; 'flavour' carries the recognition comedy for quiet surfaces. Authenticity law for this line (§9.3/§9.11): the drama is MONEY and COLD — the meter that climbs while every lamp stays green, the first visitor after quiet who pays for a stranger's deploy, the nine-minute bill — and the Denial-of-Wallet is depicted only as consequence: the rate advisory, the ticking meter, the finance reply. No dialler instructions, no payloads, no commands, no tool names-as-how-to, no technique anywhere; the recursion's mechanics stay off-page exactly as §9.11 demands, because the level 'teaches that cost can be attacked without touching availability' (§1.3), not attacking.

eraCodes.1998: Nothing on this shelf exists yet — §0.4 greys whole tech-tree branches 'not invented yet', and §1.6's era track is what turns the modem bank to scrap. The customer wants to pay only while the job runs; the era bills account-hours (§6.6's dial-up row) against a box that never sleeps. Where this pack speaks the year, it speaks the campaign's joke, not a product.
eraCodes.2008: The question is online, the answer is a cheaper box (§0.4's 2009 cell; §8.10 gloss). Nothing scales down; everything is always on; 'idle' is something a person is, not something a machine bills.
eraCodes.2016: The line's true opening rung: §5.6 gates serverless by CAPABILITY — 'Kubernetes competence + multi-tenant isolation → unlocks Container platform / PaaS, then Serverless' (verbatim) — which lands in the grid's cloud cell, not the dial-up cell. The pop is instant, the pool is sellable, and the first cold start is somebody's launch day.
eraCodes.2026: Now: warm capacity is the product, recursion is the bill, and every tenant's traffic is somebody else's latency. Same pan, hotter herd.

decision.type.serverless.name: The Mayfly Field
decision.type.serverless.codex: The functions line: invocations, not servers. Warm capacity decides, not compute — 'your visitor's experience depends on whether another visitor came recently' (§1.3). The level is a tension, not a wall: cost says scale to zero, latency says keep the pan hot, and the Chrysalis Pool is where you buy the absence of a stutter. The fastest threat never breaks uptime: a recursive function bills $40,000 in nine minutes while every lamp swears nothing happened. Cold starts are holes in the sparkle, legible at crowd level. This level teaches that cost can be attacked without touching availability.
decision.goal.serverless.binding: Warmth, not throughput: the visitor's experience depends on whether another visitor came recently, and a runaway spends money without touching availability — the hands that pre-warm the pool are the same hands that read the nine-minute invoice.
decision.scarce.serverless.qos: A warm shell outranks a cold spawn, and a share-holding tenant outranks an over-runner — the pool sheds the burst into visible frost before it ever sheds the steady field, because the sparkle is the product and the stutter is the theft. A single tenant's burst starves others only if the ladder is allowed to invert.
decision.skin.serverless.inspector: Pan black and pop yellow: the board is a field of mayflies that spawn, do one thing, and vanish in under a second, and at volume the field is a shimmer, not a crowd. A cold start is a visibly slower, duller pop with a little puff of frost; past the density line they render as dark specks — holes in the sparkle, cheaper and more legible. The Chrysalis Pool glows at the pan's rim, its fullness the meter; the money graph rides beside uptime on its own timeout-red needle. Nothing else in the game can lose without anything breaking, and that is the point (§1.3).
decision.economy.serverless.bad-month: A function that invokes itself: nine minutes, $40,000.
decision.cac.serverless.todo: §6.6 Companion B prices no serverless acquisition channel; the §0.3 customer row ('App devs') names WHO, not WHAT. Placeholder until the pricing pass — never invented.
decision.verbs.serverless.transfer.1: Metered-exposure discipline transfers everywhere: any line whose product is an act rather than a rental now asks you the same question — what does the runaway cost before anyone reaches for the cap, and who is watching a meter that can bleed you while every uptime lamp stays green?
decision.relations.serverless.mastery: The pool reads the quarter: shares sized before the first herd, the timeout budget set before the first recursion, warmth bought against the rhythm it protects rather than guessed, and the monthly meter boring enough to skim.
decision.relations.serverless.distillate: Playbook: price the act as carefully as the asset — a metered line makes success itself a threat vector; treat the absence of a stutter as a product with a purchase order behind it; and remember that a failure which never touches availability still ends companies, because a runaway bill is an outage that arrives by invoice instead of by alarm.
decision.handover.serverless.runs-out: Your warm capacity and your attention to the meter. An empty pool is a stutter you will pay for later in other people's first visitors; a full pool nobody sized is idle money burning while the field pops for free.
decision.handover.serverless.kills-you: The blast radius: one tenant's burst starving the field, or one function invoking itself and billing $40,000 in nine minutes while every availability lamp stays green — the attack that spends the company without breaking the service.
decision.handover.serverless.customer-wants: The pan already hot: sub-second pops for their first visitor, and a bill that scales with their success instead of a stranger's storm. They experience your queue only as their own latency.
decision.rosetta.serverless.shares: Concurrency shares are the cgroup cage spent against mayflies: the same bet that a bounded neighbor is cheaper than an unbounded one, sold now in units of warmth instead of memory.
decision.rosetta.serverless.warmth: The reserved-warmth level is the oversell ratio pointed at frost: shells sold past the pool's ability to keep them warm come back as visible stutters on the first arrival after quiet, not as a degraded read nobody scheduled.
decision.scenarios.serverless.recursive-invocatio: The Recursive Invocation Bill (§2.12): a function finds its own endpoint and calls itself nine minutes flat while the availability board stays green and the meter does arithmetic; the incident is the invoice. 'Denial of Wallet' in its purest form — an attacker, or a bug, spends your money without taking you down. The tell was the rate; the fix was the timeout; the lesson is that cost is an availability problem wearing a billing coat.
decision.scenarios.serverless.burst-starvation: Burst Starvation (§1.3): one tenant's launch-day graph goes vertical, the shared pool stops growing, and every other app's first visitors pay for a stranger's success in frost. The fairness law of the line made mechanical — patience set by another visitor's arrival history, and the shares you did not sell doing the shedding.
decision.scenarios.serverless.popcorn-pan: The Popcorn Pan (§1.3's own title): a promoted app's crowd arrives against a pool that just scaled down, and pops land irregularly across the field, some trailing little plumes of frost, the shimmer going patchy dark. 'Perfect for spikes, catastrophic when attacked' (§4.2) — tonight the spike is the customer's good news and nobody pre-warmed for it.
decision.alert.recursion-runaway: {functionName} on {nodeId} has been invoking itself since {hour}:{minute} — {minutesRun} minutes, meter at {billAmount}. Every availability lamp is green. That is the incident.
decision.alert.burst-starvation: One arrival history just became everyone's: {tenantsStarved} tenants behind {nodeId} paying the frost for a stranger's burst.
decision.alert.cold-pool-empty: Warm fraction {warmFraction} and falling — invocation {invocationId} waited {coldStartMs}ms for a shell that is not there. The pan is cold.
decision.alert.popcorn-herd: The field is popping faster than the pool can warm: dark specks spreading across the shimmer on {nodeId}.
decision.alert.bill-climb: Meter climb on {nodeId}: {billAmount} this hour with no availability event behind it — cost moved, and nothing else did.
decision.terms.warm-pool: The Chrysalis Pool: pre-warmed shells that shorten cold starts — 'buying warmth is buying the absence of a stutter' (§4.2 verbatim). Idle money for latency you only notice by its absence.
decision.terms.scale-to-zero: The switch that lets the pan go cold on purpose: no idle bill while nothing cooks, and the first visitor after the quiet pays the frost (§1.3/§4.2). The level's whole tension, one toggle wide.
decision.terms.per-invoke-metering: Every pop is a postmark: 'pay-per-invoke' (§4.2 verbatim) — fractions of a cent, billions of times, a meter that runs for whoever arrives: attacker, customer, or bug.
decision.refusal.hands-exhausted: Both hands are committed. The {verb} intent is queued and presents when a hand frees at tick {availableAtTick}.
decision.refusal.stamped-in-future: The {verb} intent is stamped for tick {availableAtTick}, ahead of the current minute. Nothing was spent.
decision.refusal.unknown-node: No board object named {nodeId} exists at the current tick. Nothing was changed.
decision.refusal.edge-exists: A {relationKind} cable already links {nodeId} to those endpoints. The existing edge was left as it is.
decision.refusal.slot-occupied: {slotName} on {nodeId} is occupied. One supplier per socket; disconnect before you reconnect.
decision.status.rung-5: We are aware of the fire.

flavour.ticket.subject.invoice: our bill says {billAmount} but our traffic graph looks like this
flavour.ticket.body.invoice: Ticket {ticketId}, filed {hour}:{minute} morning. Nothing broke, nothing was down, the status page stayed green all nine minutes — and the meter says {functionName} was calling itself in a closed loop nobody scheduled. They want the money. The money went calling. Finance wants a name for the cost center, which is a sentence nobody has ever enjoyed reading about a function.

flavour.ticket.body.first-visit: Everyone's first visitor paid for a stranger's deploy. The rest of the pops were instant, which somehow makes it worse — 'the first one after idle is slow and the rest are fast' is a sentence that should live in your documentation, not be explained to us at 9am by an engineer trying to be kind.

eras.2016: our overnight job ran {coldStartMs}ms late because a launch-day we never saw spent the reserved pool
eras.2026: our scheduled run landed {coldStartMs}ms late because someone ELSE's burst held the shells

ticket.subject.starved.fallback: our scheduled run landed {coldStartMs}ms late because someone ELSE's burst held the shells

flavour.ticket.body.starved: Ten minutes behind the window, every invocation queued into frost while a launch-day graph we have never seen spent the pool. The page you sold says infinite instant burst capacity. The page did not mention whose burst is instant first, or that our reliability is somebody else's traffic report.
flavour.ticket.subject.nines: who owns {functionName} — accounting wants the runaway bill explained
flavour.ticket.body.nines: It recursed for {minutesRun} minutes before anyone looked, spent {billAmount} doing it, and the endpoint it loved best was its own. Nobody owns the function; everybody owns the cost center. Please reply before finance replies to us with stronger words than 'please'.
flavour.press.headline.herd: {hostName}'s launch-day crowd outran its own warm pool — users describe 'a stutter in the sparkle'; capacity, in the end, was bought after the fact.
flavour.press.headline.bill: No outage at {hostName}, auditors confirm — only nine minutes, one recursive function, and {billAmount} moving in the wrong direction; the incident report is an invoice.
flavour.forum.thread.frost: Anyone else's cold-start graph showing {coldStartMs}ms spikes exactly after quiet periods? The plan page promises sub-second pops and technically it delivers — just not all the same second, or to the same customer.
flavour.forum.thread.shares: Whoever priced reserved warmth per shell was right and I cannot unsee it. Watched a demo pool go dark speck by speck through a burst and physically reached for a share cap on a tenant I did not own.
flavour.chatter.desk.warm: Pan's warm, field's steady, meter's boring. On this line 'boring' is the product demo.
flavour.chatter.desk.frost: Watch the shimmer: eight pops, one frost puff, no ticket yet. That is not green — that is early.
flavour.codex.warm-cold: 'Buying warmth is buying the absence of a stutter' (§4.2 verbatim): idle money for latency noticed only by its absence. The pool is a purchase of negatives — the stutter that does not happen, the ticket never filed, the first visitor who never learns your cold-start ladder exists.
flavour.codex.arrival-history: 'The only unit in the game whose patience cost is set by the arrival history of other units' (§3.3 verbatim): the mayfly before you is your problem. Fairness on this line is not kindness — it is the shedding ladder reading the history correctly while there is still a history worth reading.
flavour.loading.tip.frost: A cold start is 'a visibly slower, duller pop with a little puff of frost' (§1.3). If your users could see the board, they would know before your monitoring did.

eras.1998: There is no zero to scale to. The box hums whether anyone uses it or not, the account bills by the hour, and always-on is the whole product.
eras.2008: You want the server to stop billing when the jobs sleep. The honest era's answer: buy a smaller box and let it hum more cheaply.
eras.2016: Scale to zero is new and true: the bill stops when the pan goes cold, and the first visitor pays for the frost. The tension between cost and latency finally has a dial.
eras.2026: Scale to zero means the pan goes cold on purpose: the bill stops, and so does the warmth. 'The tension between cost and latency' (§1.3) is the level; the dial is the lesson.

loading.tip.zero.fallback: Scale to zero means the pan goes cold on purpose: the bill stops, and so does the warmth. 'The tension between cost and latency' (§1.3) is the level; the dial is the lesson.

flavour.intern.entry.pop: Day {day}: counted the pops for an hour. Nothing broke, nothing caught fire, and the boss called it the best shift since launch. The meter, she said, is the only thing that ever lies here — and it only lies by being ignored.
flavour.intern.entry.bill: Day {day}: saw the runaway invoice reprinted and taped to the console. Nine minutes. The senior tech read it twice, pinned the timeout-budget card over it, and wrote underneath: 'green lamps are not a fire alarm'.
flavour.sticky.note.timeout: Taped above the control plane: 'a self-DDoS with a bill attached'. Nobody has laughed at it since the recursion week. — console note, post-incident
flavour.abuse.canon.rate-advisory: Meter advisory: {functionName} invoked itself for {minutesRun} minutes with no external caller pattern. Exposure {billAmount}. Set a timeout and a cap before the next quiet window.
flavour.abuse.canon.customer-dispute: Formal dispute opened on ticket {ticketId}: the account denies the recursion, the rate, and the phrase 'reasonable usage'. They do not deny the function name. Legal has the toner ready.
flavour.vendor.reply.firmware: Have you tried updating to the latest firmware?
flavour.vendor.reply.log-bundle: Please collect a full log bundle.
flavour.vendor.reply.known-issue: This is a known issue, fixed in the next release (no ETA).
flavour.canary.warm-pool-tally: Pool {warmFraction}, frost {coldStartMs}ms, meter {billAmount} this hour — the herd, the freeze and the runaway are the same instrument, read three times.
